_label: Evidence archive: the studio's websites as captured by the Internet Archive (2013-2016)

identified_by.content: Evidence archive: the studio's websites as captured by the Internet Archive (2013-2016)

content: The Internet Archive holds dated captures of two domains the studio ran, and those captures are public and checkable by anyone. On www.wtfisart.com: a capture of 2013-07-20 showing only 'Under Construction:Check back soon !', and captures of 2014-12-18 and 2016-01-11 showing a site whose menu reads 'Artists', 'Art Market Reform is a happening' and 'Got Provenance ?', and whose text reads 'For the Love of God, We are the Art. Long Live the Art Spirit !', alongside the phrases 'Art is Capital invest with confidence' and 'What Hedge Funds ?! invest in Art'. On www.sunandrainworks.com: captures of 2016-01-26 and 2016-03-27 carrying the eight defining characteristics of Metaconceptual Art in full, in the same wording as the 2012 posting recorded elsewhere in this collection. What these captures establish is that the concept, its eight characteristics, and the studio's art-market vocabulary were published on the studio's own domains and preserved by a third party on dates no one in the studio controls. What they do not establish is anything about the auction of 2009: no capture mentions it, or lot 16, or Ansel Adams, or Sotheby's.

referred_to_by.content: Evidence status: third-party captures, publicly checkable, and the strongest kind of source in this collection short of an institution's own file. The captures are held by the Internet Archive at https://web.archive.org/web/20141218140553/http://wtfisart.com/ , https://web.archive.org/web/20160111165857/http://wtfisart.com/ , https://web.archive.org/web/20160126080729/http://www.sunandrainworks.com/ and https://web.archive.org/web/20160327052433/http://sunandrainworks.com/content/beginnings-art-odyssey . The capture timestamps are the Archive's own and are not the studio's to set; that is what makes them evidence. Two things inside the pages are not: the content management system's 'Submitted by' stamps, which a site owner can set or change, and the page text itself, which is the studio's writing. So the dates to cite are the capture dates, and the stamps are reported as what the site said of itself.

What the wtfisart.com captures show, and how little it is. The earliest capture of the domain, 2010-01-25, is not a page: it is a redirect, sent by a web server that named itself as serving wtfisart.com, to a generic page on securepaynet.net, a domain of the registrar's hosting service, so a hosting account existed but served no studio content. The next, 2011-02-10, is a parked advertising page with no studio content. Neither says anything about what the site carried in 2009: the registrar's receipts record shows the domain was registered for one year on 2009-03-16 and not renewed in the year that followed, so by the 2011 capture it had lapsed, and registrars commonly park a lapsed address. The studio registered the name again on 2011-10-16, eight months after the 2011 capture, which is why the captures below resume. On 2013-07-20 the domain carries one line, 'Under Construction:Check back soon !', on a page the studio wrote itself; the passage below sets out how that is told apart from the parked captures around it. By 2014-12-18, and still on 2016-01-11, it carries a Drupal installation whose main menu reads 'Artists', 'Art Market Reform is a happening' and 'Got Provenance ?'. The body text is the same paragraph repeated in three panels, ending 'For the Love of God, We are the Art. Long Live the Art Spirit !', and the page states 'Welcome to wtfisart.com. No front page content has been created yet.' That last sentence should be quoted by anyone citing this record. What was captured is a demonstration installation carrying the studio's slogans in its menu, not a working publication. Its value is narrow and real: on a date fixed by a third party, the studio was publicly calling a work of its own a happening, and was publishing the line that is handwritten on the Art Notes board.

The slider on the 2014 site carries three of the studio's paintings. The site of 2014-12-18, and unchanged on 2016-01-11, runs Drupal under a theme called CorporateClean, and its three slider images are requested from sites/all/themes/corporateclean/mockup/, which is where that theme ships its own sample pictures. The files served from those paths are not the theme's samples. They are photographs of paintings: slide-1 carries the words 'Art is Capital', slide-2 'ART MARKET REFORM', and slide-3 'what hedge funds ?', each in painted letters across a worked ground. All three are archived and can be fetched: 81,058, 93,694 and 86,711 bytes, each 500 by 250 pixels. Above them the slider headings read 'Art Market Reform is a happening', 'Art is Capital invest with confidence' and 'What Hedge Funds ?! invest in Art'. So three paintings are dated to the studio's own site by a third party, twice, thirteen months apart.

The Art Market Reform on the site is not the one published here. The painting in slide-2 is lettered across a blue ground worked with white, and the painting published with this collection's Art Market Reform record is a different object: the words set over a dense multicoloured ground, with 'Art' in block letters and 'Market Reform' in script. They are two paintings sharing a title, not two photographs of one painting. The studio has said its works exist and are held in its collection; this capture shows that at least one title names more than one object, which any fuller record of these works will have to describe as a set.

What the slider does not establish, stated so the capture is not asked to carry more than it can. The three images are 500 by 250 pixels, a banner shape, so each is a crop and none documents a whole painting. The capture dates the photographs' presence on the site and nothing about when the paintings were made. The same page carries Drupal's untouched message that no front page content has been created yet, so the installation was only partly configured, and the slider headings sit above the theme's own placeholder paragraph repeated three times. By the capture of 2016-10-09 the site had been rebuilt on Open Atrium and the slider was gone.

The phrase that runs through the site, and the studio's account of it. The body text of the 2014 and 2016 captures ends 'For the Love of God, We are the Art. Long Live the Art Spirit !'. The studio states, in 2026, that this was by design: that the sign-off 'For the Love of Art', which closes its approaches of August 2008 and its note returning the signed consignment agreement in March 2009, and the line 'For the love of God, We are th[...]!' on the Art Notes panel, and this sentence on the website, are one chain rather than three separate flourishes. The objective record is consistent with that and does not establish it: the sign-off is documented in the correspondence of 2008 and 2009, the panel line is photographed in a file dated 2012, and this is the phrase's earliest appearance in a third-party capture. Which came first in intention is the studio's statement, not the documents'. The studio further states that 'Long Live the Art Spirit' comes from Robert Henri's The Art Spirit, the collection of his teaching published in 1923, which it says it read around 2006. Nothing here dates that reading, and the phrase's earliest dated appearance in this collection is this capture of 2014-12-18.

The capture of 2013-07-20 is not a parked page, and the captures on either side of it are. This matters more than the one line of text it carries, so the three are set out together as the archive serves them. On 2011-02-10 the address answers with a frameset pointing at sedoparking.com, a domain-parking service. On 2014-01-05 it answers with a single full-page iframe pointing at a GoDaddy parking path. Between them, on 2013-07-20, it answers with eleven lines of hand-written HTML: a doctype, a title reading 'Under Construction:Check back soon !', a background colour set inline to #00ccff, and one image tag for underconstruction.png at 842 by 443 pixels. There is no advertising frame, no registrar iframe and no third-party script, and the image is requested by a relative path, so it was being served from the domain itself rather than from a parking provider. Whoever held the address in July 2013 had put their own page on it. That is a stronger statement than the earlier reading of this capture, which took it for a bare holding page and did not distinguish it from the parked ones.

What that capture still does not establish, which is most of what one would want. The page carries no name, no studio, no mention of art and no link: nothing in it identifies its author. The inference that it is the studio's rests on the registration rather than on the page, because the receipts record has the studio registering wtfisart.com again on 2011-10-16, and the address is serving hand-made content within that later registration rather than within the lapse that preceded it. The studio's own account, given in 2026, is that the page was its own and in its own style of the time. That account is recorded as the studio's; the page cannot confirm it. The image the page displayed was never captured: a query for underconstruction.png returns no result at any timestamp, so the only picture on the page is the one thing about it that cannot be examined. And the parked capture of 2014-01-05 shows that whatever was being built in July 2013 was not being served six months later, which is worth keeping in view beside the Drupal site that appears at the end of that year.

What the sunandrainworks.com captures show. The root capture of 2013-05-22 is a bare Drupal installation with no content. By 2016-01-26 the front page carries two posts, and the page 'Beginnings of an Art Odyssey', captured separately on 2016-03-27, sets out all eight defining characteristics of Metaconceptual Art in full: the returning of the formless to form; the commodification of art and its relation to the global economic crisis; the power structures of the art world and its institutions; an archaeology of the art world and art history; the interplay of time and space; transcendence of medium to arrive within the collective consciousness; the annihilating of the boundaries between art-world insiders and outsiders; and the annihilating of the boundaries between art and life. This is the same set, in the same order and substantially the same words, as the posting of 2012 recorded in the postings evidence record, which is itself independently preserved. The site's own stamps give 'Submitted by Rainbow on Sun, 10/04/2015' for that page and 'Fri, 11/14/2014' for its sibling; those are the site's account of itself, and the capture dates are the part no one in the studio controls.

The Flickr account, and the photograph of the notice board. The studio's public Flickr account, under the display name Joe Chirum and the user name LivingArt8, was joined in March 2008 and holds some seven hundred photographs, most of them the studio's tie-dye and batik work and its paintings. It is a working photostream rather than a record of this project, and nothing in it should be read as evidence about the auction. One photograph in it does bear on this collection: the notice board published here as Art Notes, titled 'Art Notes' and marked 'Uploaded on June 2, 2013', at https://www.flickr.com/photos/24377024@N07/8921139312/ . The image is pixel-identical to the studio's held original. So the board, with the line 'WTF is Art ?!' on it, was publicly posted on a third party's platform three months before the museum letter of 2013-09-12, at an address anyone can check, on a date the platform assigned and the studio did not. It was not, on any evidence here, publicly read: that page records eight views in the thirteen years since. Flickr's 'Taken on June 1, 2013' on that photograph is not a capture date: it is the value Flickr supplies when an uploaded file carries no Exif, and the copy uploaded had been stripped. The studio's own original gives 2012-11-30, and the Art Notes record sets out how that date is bounded.

What else the photostream carries, enumerated on 2026-09-12, with its dates and its limits. Nine photographs in the account bear on this collection, and their upload dates fall in two groups. On 2013-06-02, in the same upload session as the Art Notes board, the account posted a digital work titled 'ArtHistoriansOTheFuture', at https://www.flickr.com/photos/24377024@N07/8920785186/ , which is the inscription of a studio board recoloured over a rainbow ground and whose words recur in the museum letter of 2013-09-12; the inscription-photograph record describes the board it was made from, photographed in 2011. The same session posted a painting titled 'WhatHedgeFunds(AcryliconCardboard)', at https://www.flickr.com/photos/24377024@N07/8921172858/ . That is a work carrying the title What Hedge Funds, publicly posted three months before the museum letter. The registrar's receipts record independently dates the registration of WHATHEDGEFUNDS.COM to 2011-10-16, and the 2014 capture described above shows the studio's own site publishing the line 'What Hedge Funds ?! invest in Art'. Three unrelated third parties - a photo host, a domain registrar and the Internet Archive - therefore fix three separate dates against that one title, and the studio set none of them. On 2014-05-18 the account posted six further works: 'ArtMarketReform7x10Watercolor' and 'ArtMarketReform9x12Acrylic', 'ArtTax7x10Watercolor1' and 'ArtTax7x10Watercolor2', and 'WhatHedgeFunds12x16Acrylic' and 'WhatHedgeFunds6x8Acrylic', with media and dimensions given in the titles and, on three of them, in a description field reading 'Acrylic on Canvas' or 'Mixed Media'. Art Market Reform and Art Tax are the two works the museum letter of 2013-09-12 names as Metaconceptual Art. These photographs postdate that letter by eight months, so they are consistent with it and are not evidence for it: what they establish is that the works the letter named exist as physical objects, not that they existed when it was written. Three of the 2014 photographs carry the public tag 'Metaconceptual'. That is the earliest publicly published use of the term located anywhere in this collection whose date is assigned by a third party - the 2013 letter is earlier but was private correspondence, and the profile biography that uses the term is undated and unarchived. One caution applies to all eight files: each shows a 'Taken on' value exactly one day before its upload date, which is Flickr's fallback for a file carrying no Exif. None of them carries a camera date, and the upload stamp is the only date any of them has.

The Flickr biography, and why it carries no date. The same account's profile biography states that in May 2009 the artist auctioned an artwork at a Sotheby's New York photograph auction, lot 16, 'as a performance act of metaconceptual Art', titled 'WTF is Ansel Adams ?!'. That is the designation this collection records, in the artist's own words, on a public page. It cannot be dated. A profile biography can be rewritten at any time and keeps no visible history, and the Internet Archive holds no capture of this profile at all, which was checked on 2026-09-11. It is therefore a public assertion of unknown date, and it repeats the same error as the 2013 letter in giving the sale as May 2009 when the catalogue gives 30 March 2009. Both are left as they stand, for the reason the museum correspondence record sets out.

What is not the studio's, and must not be cited as if it were. The domain wtfisart.com passed out of the studio's hands. A capture of 2016-07-11 shows a hosting suspension page, and from 2020 the domain carries an unrelated publication of art, film and book reviews written under several bylines, which is captured many hundreds of times between 2020 and 2025. The registry record was checked in 2026 and shows a fresh registration of 2024-08-29, so the domain lapsed and was taken up again by someone else. Nothing captured from 2016-07 onward is the studio's work, and the later site's contents say nothing about this collection. A separate incarnation captured on 2016-11-02, a wiki-style 'encyclopedic directory of Art' listing artists, is recorded here only so that a reader who finds it is not misled: it names no work of the studio's and makes no claim this collection relies on.

What this record does not show. None of these captures mentions the auction of 30 March 2009, lot 16, Ansel Adams, Sotheby's, or any performance act; the only public statement of that designation on these platforms is the undated Flickr biography. Nothing here bears on the 2007 origin asserted elsewhere in this collection. And the 2014 menu item 'Art Market Reform is a happening' is evidence that the studio used the word publicly of a work of its own on a date a third party fixed; it is not evidence of what the studio meant by the word in 2008, which the museum-approach record weighs separately.
